content: The rulers spoke French, and so did
power. For three hundred years after
1066 the law, the government, the war,
the church and the kitchens of the great
houses ran in French, while the English
went on speaking English to each other.
Tier 2 is those domains, the courts first.
accuse     beside the plain brand
judge      beside the older deem
crime      beside the older wrong
sentence   beside the older doom
Deem and doom are what an English judge
once did and what he handed down.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: law and justice.
The rest of the courtroom. Almost every
word in it is French, and almost every
one had an English word already doing
the work.
acquit    beside the plain free
detain    beside the plain hold
warrant   beside the older writ
felon     beside the Norse outlaw
English law never chose between the two
layers. It says both at once: a will and
testament, goods and chattels. The plain
word for the man, the French word for
the record.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: law and justice.
King and queen are English words. Nearly
everything a king does is French: he
reigns, he is royal and sovereign, he
governs, he issues a decree.
govern     beside the plain steer
mayor      beside the older reeve
council    beside the older moot
nation     beside the older land
The witan was the assembly of wise men
who advised an English king. Parliament
replaced it, from parler, to talk.
The reeve who ran an English town is
still inside sheriff, the shire's reeve.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: government.
The ranks of the conquerors and the land
they held by them. Duke and baron are
Norman words. Of the English titles only
earl came through, and it was set below
the Norman duke.
duke       beside the older earl
baron      beside the older lord
province   beside the older shire
vassal     beside the older thane
The earl kept his own title and lost his
wife's. She is a countess, from the
French comte, because English had no
feminine to set beside earl.
THE NEXT 21 CARDS: rank and land.
War was the Normans' trade and the words
of the trade are theirs: army, battle,
siege, assault, conquer. What stayed
English is what a man held in his hands:
sword, shield, spear, bow.
army      beside the older men
battle    beside the older fight
archer    beside the older bowman
lance     beside the older spear
Host is still the word for a great
company, though it has gone to church:
the heavenly host is an army.
THE NEXT 21 CARDS: war and conflict.
The castle, the camp and the field: the
gear and the ranks of a Norman army.
banner    beside the plain flag
moat      beside the older ditch
armour     beside the older shield
bugle     beside the older horn
Two English words for a boy in service
went opposite ways. Cniht rose to be the
knight, a mounted lord. Cnafa sank to be
the knave, a scoundrel, and the French
sergeant took the job he had left.
THE NEXT 22 CARDS: war and conflict.
The English kept the animals and the
Normans ate them. In the field the beast
has its old English name; on the table
the same beast is French.
beef      beside the living cow
pork      beside the living pig
mutton    beside the living sheep
boil      beside the older seethe
Nobody planned it. It is only who was in
the yard and who was at the table, set
into the language and left there.
THE NEXT 19 CARDS: food and kitchen.
The rest of the kitchen: what the meat
was cooked in, and what was set beside
it.
veal      beside the living calf
venison   beside the living deer
sugar     beside the older honey
cauldron  beside the older kettle
Honey was England's sweetener until
sugar came, and sugar came in French.
Ginger was here before the Normans, as
the Old English gingifer. The French
form is the one that stayed.
THE NEXT 19 CARDS: food and kitchen.
The English had clothes. The Normans had
fashion, and the whole of this cluster
is the difference: a garment is a thing
to wear, attire is a thing to be seen
in.
garment   beside the older cloth
gown      beside the older smock
jewel     beside the plain stone
brooch    beside the plain pin
The kirtle was the English gown and it
is gone. Cloth stayed, because somebody
still had to weave it.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: cloth and fashion.
Ribbon, velvet, brocade, chiffon: the
cloths came in by French trade and so
did their names. The English word for
precious cloth, godwebb, is gone
without a trace.
ribbon   beside band, the Norse tie
cotton   beside the older linen
scarlet  beside the plain red
plume    beside the plain feather
Reek once meant smoke and nothing worse.
Perfume took the pleasant half of the
work and left reek the rest.
THE NEXT 16 CARDS: the fine stuffs.
England had been Christian for four
centuries and more before the Normans
came, so the plain words of the faith
were already English: church, priest,
bishop, minster. What arrived in 1066
was the management of it.
abbey    beside the older minster
chapel   beside the older church
vicar    beside the older priest
diocese  beside the bishopric
Shrift was the English word for
confession. It survives in short shrift,
the brief hearing given to a man about
to be hanged.
THE NEXT 19 CARDS: the church.
The second half of the church: what
stands in it, and what it teaches.
saint     beside the holy one
crucifix  beside the older rood
paradise  beside the older heaven
sermon    beside the plain speech
Rood was the English word for the cross.
It stands in the rood screen still, and
it named Holyrood.
The nave of a church is the Latin navis,
a ship: the body of the building likened
to an upturned hull.
THE NEXT 17 CARDS: the church.
An Englishman had a house. A Norman had
a manor, and the rooms inside it took
French names as fast as they were built.
manor      beside the homestead
chamber    beside the older room
cellar     beside the undercroft
fence      beside the older hedge
The English hall let its smoke out at a
hole in the roof. Chimney is the French
word for the thing that replaced it.
The parlour is the room for talking, from
parler, exactly as parliament is.
THE NEXT 16 CARDS: house and property.
The rest of the great house and the yard
behind it. Most of these words name a
part of a building grander than an
English farm had any use for.
wardrobe   beside the plain chest
pantry     beside the bread room
closet     beside the cupboard
cottage    beside the plain hut
A wardrobe was a room before it was a
piece of furniture: ward and robe, the
place where the robes were guarded. A
pantry is a bread room, from pain.
THE NEXT 15 CARDS: house and property.
